description: Critical Load is an Ontario Tech team of nuclear, mechanical, and software engineering students taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We’re building a tool that uses NASA lunar terrain and ephemeris data to compare south pole landing sites by sunlight, power potential, and Earth communication windows, and flags where solar falls short and fission surface power could fill the gap.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free web app that answers the two questions every lander at the Moon's south pole depends on: will it have sunlight for power, and can it see Earth to radio home? Pick a site and a date, and the app shows the Sun and Earth against the real horizon, with a plain GO / CAUTION / NO-GO verdict. At the south pole, where Artemis plans to land, the Sun skims the horizon, so hills and crater rims decide everything. Using NASA LOLA terrain, the app shows how a site that looks sunny on a smooth Moon can be NO-GO in reality, and how sites a few kilometres apart differ. It also simulates 1,000 landings around a target to estimate the chance of a safe touchdown, and can search nearby for better spots. Built for mission planners: when a launch slip or hardware change moves the landing date or site, it reruns the power, communication and landing checks in seconds, work that today means stepping through Quickmap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons by hand. It is a fast first check before detailed analysis, with Sun and Earth positions checked against NASA JPL Horizons (750 points, within 0.007°). Its plain verdicts also help educators show why the south pole is so hard.
details: Live app: https://critical-load.vercel.app | Code and full README: https://github.com/washmaz/critical-load | User and Technical Guide (PDF): https://critical-load.vercel.app/critical-load-guide.pdf. Pick any lunar site and landing time; the app checks Sun and Earth against NASA LOLA terrain horizons and gives GO / CAUTION / NO-GO for power and direct-to-Earth comms. It runs 1,000 Monte Carlo touchdowns, lets power, comms, landing, thermal, science and mission planning teams set their own limits and weights, ranks sites, and flags clashes. Sun/Earth positions use JPL DE421 tables with a live JPL Horizons cross-check (750 points, max 0.007 deg). Built with React, three.js and astronomy-engine on free NASA data. Use of AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped write code, docs and the demo; demo voice-over is AI text-to-speech.
